name: clisp
desc: GNU CLISP, a Common Lisp implementation
why: An old-school Common Lisp implementation with a long history and a REPL that rewards exploration.

brief.what_it_is: GNU CLISP is a free implementation of ANSI Common Lisp, distributed as a single clisp program. Run with no arguments it starts an interactive read-eval-print loop on standard input and output. It can also compile Lisp files to bytecode (.fas) with -c, run expressions with -x, or run a Lisp file as a script. The homepage calls it a feature-loaded implementation of the language. The brew formula also installs a clisp-link executable.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents CLISP as a complete, standards-conforming Common Lisp environment that is free software, and offers ANSI Common Lisp as a programming environment. The manual adds that it is meant for interactive exploration and scripting, not only for batch compilation.
brief.how_it_works: The clisp executable is a startup driver that finds the runtime (lisp.run) and starts it with the right arguments. The runtime loads an initial memory image (lisp.mem) that holds the Lisp-implemented part of CLISP, and the C runtime handles the rest. Setup is controlled by a run-control file, .clisprc.lisp, in the home directory, which loads on startup unless -norc is given. The manual says the REPL supports TAB completion, and that typing a space after a symbol describes the current function.

Option summary: runs the given Lisp expressions in batch mode instead of the REPL, printing their values. The manual notes that the shell requires the expressions to be wrapped in double quotes with inner quotes and backslashes escaped.
Option summary: compiles the named Lisp file to bytecode (*.fas) in batch mode. The compiled file can then be loaded in place of the source.

Option summary: loads and runs a Lisp file as a script, with no REPL. The first line may start with #! to use CLISP as an interpreter. -norc is listed among the options; its manual entry says it skips the run-control file.
Listed under the REPL's command-line environment: lists symbols whose names match name. Typed at the CLISP prompt, not the shell.
Listed under the REPL's command-line environment: describes the given symbol. Typed at the CLISP prompt.

brief.install_notes: The brew formula is named clisp and installs clisp and clisp-link. The homepage also lists packages for Debian, Fedora, Gentoo, Arch, Ubuntu, the BSDs, MacPorts, Fink, Cygwin and CSW. No hardware, accounts, or runtimes are needed beyond the binary. Building from source uses ./configure with options such as --cbc build, which the manual recommends for a clean build. Optional per-user setup goes in ~/.clisprc.lisp, and the manual says environment variables such as LANG and CLISP_LANGUAGE set the interface language.
brief.standout: CLISP is a full ANSI Common Lisp with a long history, and its REPL has built-in discovery: TAB completion that changes with context, and APROPOS and DESCRIBE for exploring symbols. It can also be used as a login shell, according to the homepage, which is unusual for a Lisp.
brief.status: Quiet, by the evidence I could see. The homepage says the current version is 2.49, dated 2010-07-07, and the manual's footer has the same date. The homepage still links development to a Mercurial repository and nightly implementation notes. I did not check the Homebrew formula's version or the upstream release history, so I can't confirm the current release.
brief.caveats: The homepage and manual are both dated 2010 and describe version 2.49, so the documentation may lag the current code. The manual's Unix-focused options and the note that other platforms are similar suggest Unix is the main target. The homepage says it is not backed by any company and depends on donations. Licensing is GNU GPL, with the documentation under GFDL. The manual says the default memory is 3 MB, and that the -x option needs careful shell quoting. The homepage was reachable, and no build problems were visible from the pages I read.
